html:
The Indus script is the set of signs used by the Indus Valley civilisation from about 2600 to 1900 BCE. It has never been deciphered.

The signs appear mostly on small square stamp seals of carved stone, often above an animal such as a "unicorn", a bull or an elephant, and also on pottery, tablets, copper tools and a large signboard at Dholavira. About 400 to 600 different signs are known. Most inscriptions are very short, with an average of about five signs, and none is long.

That shortness is the main problem. There is no bilingual text, like the Rosetta Stone for Egyptian hieroglyphs, and we do not know what language the Indus people spoke. Proposals link it to early Dravidian, to an Indo-Aryan language or to a lost language; a few scholars argue it is not full writing at all.

Seals with the script turn up in Mesopotamia, evidence of trade with Sumer and Indus seals in Mesopotamia. The script disappeared as the cities declined, and India had no known writing again until the Edicts of Ashoka.
sum: The Indus script is the set of signs used by the Indus Valley civilisation from about 2600 to 1900 BCE. It has never been deciphered.
